GoScheme now compiles to bytecode and runs on a stack machine.  Programs are
compiled by default; `-interp` runs the tree-walker instead, which is how the
two are compared, and `docs/bytecode.md` is the long version of everything
below.

```sh
goscheme script.scm                  # compiled where possible (the default)
goscheme -interp script.scm          # the tree-walker, for comparison
goscheme compile script.scm          # writes script.scmc
goscheme script.scmc                 # runs bytecode; the source is not read
goscheme build script.scm            # a standalone executable holding bytecode
```

### Running a script compiles it

This is worth saying plainly because it was not true before: `goscheme
script.scm` used to hand the whole file to the compiler as **one body**, and a
body the compiler cannot translate is not translated at all.  One `import` at
the top — which every real script has — was enough to send the entire file to
the tree-walker, silently.  `load`, library files and the embedded extensions
went the same way.

Now a file is compiled form by form, in one continuation extent, wherever it
comes from: the command line, `load`, an `import`ed library, or `goscheme
build`.  The test suites go through the same path, and that is how the change
announced itself — the first time the suites were really compiled they found
three defects that only the compiled path could have:

* `(case key ((a b) 'x) (else => (lambda (k) k)))` — the `=>` of an `else`
  clause compiled as two body expressions, so the procedure was returned
  instead of applied;
* a macro that defines a macro (the R7RS suite's `be-like-begin1`) — the forms
  after it were compiled before the macro it defines existed, so using it
  compiled into a call to a binding that turned out to be syntax;
* `(let ((=> #f)) (cond (#t => 'ok)))` — `=>` bound as a *variable* is not the
  auxiliary keyword, and the compiler only asked the global environment, so it
  applied `'ok`.

### It is the same language

The compiler does not imitate the interpreter for a form it cannot translate:
it **declines the whole body**, and that body runs interpreted.  The two paths
therefore agree by construction, and the tests are there to prove the
construction right rather than to hope.  46 programs — every derived form, tail
calls, a 200 000-deep non-tail recursion, `call/cc` escapes and re-entries,
`dynamic-wind`, macros, records, `parameterize`, `match`, errors — run **three
ways**: compiled, compiled-to-bytes-and-back, and interpreted, and all three
have to print the same thing.  The R7RS reference suite and every extension
suite run **twice**, once per path.

What the compiler does not handle yet: `do` (deliberately — its `(continue)` is
a guard the interpreter installs, and compiling it would quietly change what
`(continue)` means), `guard`, `parameterize`, `dynamic-wind`,
`define-record-type`, `match`, `define-values`, `let-values`, `quasiquote`,
`case-lambda`, `delay` and `import`.  A body that uses one of them is
interpreted, all the way through; at the top level that is per form, so a file
still compiles form by form and a 44-form program compiles 42 of them.

### It is faster, and here is the honest table

Twelve workloads, both paths, best of three runs, on a 12th-generation i3.
Each figure includes building the machine and compiling the program:

| | bytecode | tree-walker | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lists` | 67.9 ms | 339.1 ms | **4.99×** |
| `higher-order` | 16.2 ms | 59.1 ms | **3.65×** |
| `mini-eval` | 15.5 ms | 55.2 ms | **3.56×** |
| `locals` | 53.7 ms | 191.3 ms | **3.56×** |
| `sort` | 7.7 ms | 26.4 ms | **3.43×** |
| `vectors` | 27.1 ms | 90.4 ms | **3.34×** |
| `tail-loop` | 47.0 ms | 154.4 ms | **3.28×** |
| `globals` | 54.5 ms | 175.9 ms | **3.23×** |
| `callcc` | 8.5 ms | 21.2 ms | **2.48×** |
| `fib` | 5.5 ms | 13.2 ms | **2.40×** |
| `closures` | 13.1 ms | 30.7 ms | **2.36×** |
| `strings` | 5.8 ms | 7.7 ms | **1.33×** |

Geometric mean **3.0×**, and **82% fewer bytes allocated**.  Bindings are
resolved at compile time; macros are expanded once instead of on every
evaluation; a call to a builtin such as `+` or `car` builds no continuation
frame at all; a call to a compiled procedure replaces the current activation
instead of recursing, so a non-tail recursion a million deep costs two Go stack
frames; and `cond`, `case`, `and` and `or` are jumps by the time they run.

Two caveats worth having.  These are microbenchmarks of specific shapes, not a
suite of real programs — the two closest to "a real program" are `mini-eval`
and `sort`, at 3.56× and 3.43×.  And the comparison is against *this*
tree-walker: one that cached resolved bindings and pre-expanded macros would
close part of the gap, which is precisely the point — those decisions are now
made once, ahead of time, and written to a file.

### `.scmc` files, and standalone executables

`goscheme compile` writes the compiled program, and a `.scmc` file runs without
being parsed as source.  `goscheme build` now binds the **compiled** program
into the executable instead of the script, so a built program starts without
reading source either; a script the build machine cannot compile — one that
imports a library only present when the program runs — is bound as source, and
`build` says so.  The format is versioned and a file from a newer version is
refused rather than misread.

### Three from using the REPL, and from writing a terminal program

* **Ctrl-C could not get you out of a half-written expression.**  The editor
  returned an empty line for it, which the read-eval-print loop took for "keep
  typing", so the continuation prompt came back and the only way out was to
  close the input — which reported `unexpected end of input`.  Ctrl-C now says
  what it is, and the loop throws the unfinished expression away and gives you
  the primary prompt back.
* A bracketed paste was inserted at the **end** of the line whatever the cursor
  was — the editor appended the bytes and moved the cursor to the end.  It now
  goes where the cursor is, as it does in a shell, and the line is redrawn
  around it.
* `"\033[31m"` — the way every other language writes an ANSI colour — came out
  as NUL followed by `33[31m`: the reader had `\0` but no octal escape.  String
  escapes now include C-style `\NNN`, `\e` for ESC, and `\xHH` without the
  R7RS semicolon, so a program that colours its output can be written the way it
  is written everywhere else.

### The bugs this work found

Writing the benchmark panel turned up three defects in `cond`'s code generation
that only the compiled path could have: a clause with a body popped its test
value twice, the `else` clause popped a value that was never pushed, and a
chain of failed clauses left its tests on the stack until the first one ended up
in operator position — `attempt to apply non-procedure #f`.  Nothing in the
corpus or the suites used a plain `cond`, which is why the panel found them.

Adding the multiple-values case to the corpus found a second one, older than
this work: `(lambda args ...)` — a rest parameter and nothing else — set the
rest slot but never made the name visible to the body, so it compiled as a
*global* reference and the procedure failed with `unbound variable args` the
first time it was called.  The interpreter never had the bug, which is exactly
why it went unnoticed.
